summary: Using the internet, phone or other electronic means to repeatedly harass, intimidate or spy on someone, causing fear or serious distress, can be a federal crime (18 U.S.C. 2261A). States have their own stalking laws too.

Under the federal Safe Connections Act you can ask your mobile carrier to move your line off a shared plan within 2 business days, with no fee and no approval from the account holder. Some documentation is needed.

Civil protective (restraining) orders come from state courts, so the rules differ by state. You apply at a courthouse. WomensLaw.org has state-by-state details. An order is not a substitute for a safety plan.

Under federal law (18 U.S.C. 2265), a valid protection order from one state must be honored and enforced in every other state and on tribal land, even if you have moved and have not registered it there.

The National Domestic Violence Hotline (1-800-799-7233) does not give legal advice but can help you find free local legal help. WomensLaw.org explains each state's protective order and custody laws in plain language.

In New York you can ask for an order of protection in Family Court (a civil case started with a family offense petition), in criminal court, or in Supreme Court during a divorce. It can order no contact with you.

In New York, stalking, aggravated harassment, identity theft, coercion and sharing intimate images without consent are 'family offenses' when done by a family or household member, so Family Court can hear them.
Since 2020, a New York court issuing an order of protection can also bar the other person from remotely controlling connected devices (smart home technology) in your home.
New York law lets a victim of domestic violence end another person's access to a car's connected services, such as GPS location and remote app controls.

In a New York Family Court protection order case, if you cannot afford a lawyer the court must appoint one at no cost to you. The NYS hotline (800-942-6906, text 844-997-2121) can connect you to local legal advocacy.

In England and Wales, repeated controlling or coercive behaviour by a partner or family member is a crime (Serious Crime Act 2015 s.76). Prosecutors' guidance lists monitoring you online or with spyware as an example.

Stalking is a crime in England and Wales. The law's own examples include monitoring someone's use of the internet, email or other electronic communication, and spying on them (Protection from Harassment Act 1997 s.2A).
Deliberately getting into a computer, phone or online account without authorisation is a criminal offence across the UK under the Computer Misuse Act 1990 (section 1).

The Domestic Abuse Act 2021 defines domestic abuse to include controlling or coercive behaviour, economic abuse and psychological or emotional abuse, not just physical violence. A single incident can count.

If you have experienced domestic abuse you can apply to the family court for a non-molestation order (stops harm or threats) or an occupation order (who lives in the home). No fee to apply; breaking it can mean arrest.

Legal aid may be available for domestic abuse cases if you have evidence (e.g. from police, courts or a refuge) and cannot afford legal costs. Rights of Women runs free legal advice lines for women in England and Wales.
